f-date.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-oracle-first.claim: Before the invasion, Athenian envoys at Delphi received a terrifying first answer from the priestess Aristonice: flee to the ends of the earth.

f-oracle-second.claim: The envoys returned as suppliants carrying olive branches and were given a second answer: Zeus grants that a wooden wall alone shall not be taken.

f-oracle-salamis.claim: The second answer also said: divine Salamis, you will destroy the children of women.

f-oracle-hedge.claim: Some older Athenians believed the wooden wall meant the thorn hedge that once ringed the Acropolis.

f-oracle-ships.claim: Others said the wooden wall meant the ships, and Themistocles argued the oracle would have said 'cruel Salamis', not 'divine', if Athenians were meant to die there.

f-oracle-vote.claim: The Athenians decided to meet the invader at sea with their ships, together with the other Greeks who were willing.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-laurium.claim: Years earlier Themistocles had persuaded Athens to spend a rich new silver strike from the Laurium mines on warships instead of sharing the money out.

f-laurium-number.claim: Herodotus says the silver built 200 ships.

f-evacuation.claim: The Athenians evacuated their families and slaves to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis.

f-defenders.claim: A few Athenians, the temple stewards and poor men, stayed on the Acropolis behind a barricade of planks and timber, believing it was the wooden wall of the oracle.

f-burned.claim: They killed the defenders, plundered the temple and set the whole Acropolis on fire.

f-narrows.claim: In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.
